reference_title: Wood Handbook: Wood as an Engineering Material (USDA Forest Products Laboratory, General Technical Report FPL-GTR-282, 2021)
chapter_title: Moisture Relations and Physical Properties of Wood

sections.title: Wood-Moisture Relationships
sections.summary: Wood is hygroscopic: its moisture content responds to the surrounding relative humidity and temperature. Introduces moisture content on an ovendry-weight basis and the average green moisture content by species (Table 4-1).
sections.body: Wood, like many natural materials, is hygroscopic; it gains or loses moisture to come into equilibrium with the surrounding environment. Moisture content (MC) is expressed as a percentage of ovendry weight. The average moisture content of green heartwood and sapwood varies by species (Table 4-1) and is considerable within and between trees.
key_points: Wood is hygroscopic -- moisture content responds to ambient relative humidity and temperature
Moisture content is expressed as a percentage of ovendry weight
Green heartwood/sapwood moisture content varies widely by species (Table 4-1)
sections.applicability: Establishing the moisture-content basis used throughout the chapter's equations and tables.

sections.title: Fiber Saturation and Maximum Moisture Content
sections.summary: Defines the fiber saturation point (FSP), the moisture content at which cell walls are saturated with bound water but no free water exists in the cell lumina; below FSP, most wood properties begin to change with moisture content. Gives closed-form estimates for maximum possible moisture content and the moisture content at which wood just sinks in water, both from basic specific gravity.
sections.body: [p. 4-2] Moisture can exist in wood as free water (liquid water or water vapor in cell lumina and cavities) or as bound water (held by intermolecular attraction within cell walls). The moisture content at which only the cell walls are completely saturated (all bound water) but no water exists in cell lumina is called the fiber saturation point (FSP), MCfs. The fiber saturation point is conceptually simple; however, in practice the exact partition between free and bound water [p. 4-3] is difficult to measure, and a robust operational definition is still debated. From a practical standpoint, the fiber saturation point is considered as that moisture content above which the physical and mechanical properties of wood do not change as a function of moisture content. The point below which most wood properties start to change averages about 30% moisture content, but in individual species and individual pieces of wood it can vary by several percentage points from that value. The FSP value also varies depending on the method used to measure it. Basic specific gravity Gb (ovendry mass and green volume) is the major determinant of maximum moisture content; maximum moisture content MCmax (Eq. 4-3, with the specific gravity of wood cell walls taken as 1.54) varies from 267% at Gb = 0.30 to 44% at Gb = 0.90 and is seldom attained in living trees. The moisture content at which wood will sink in water, MCsink, is given by Eq. 4-4.
key_points: The fiber saturation point is the moisture content above which physical and mechanical properties do not change with moisture content (p. 4-3)
The point below which most properties start to change averages about 30% moisture content but can vary by several percentage points by species, piece and measurement method (p. 4-3)
MCmax (Eq. 4-3) varies from 267% at Gb = 0.30 to 44% at Gb = 0.90 (p. 4-3)
MCsink (Eq. 4-4) is the moisture content at which wood will sink in water (p. 4-3)
sections.applicability: Setting the fiber-saturation-point basis (default 30%) used throughout the chapter's shrinkage equations, and bounding achievable moisture content from specific gravity alone.

sections.title: Water Vapor Sorption / Equilibrium Moisture Content
sections.summary: Equilibrium moisture content (EMC), the moisture content at which wood is neither gaining nor losing moisture, as a function of relative humidity and temperature (Fig. 4-1, Table 4-2, calculated from Eq. 4-5); an alternative equation (Eq. 4-6, Glass and others 2014) and its inverse (Eq. 4-7); the limits of Table 4-2; sorption hysteresis; automated sorption balances and sorption kinetics.
sections.body: [p. 4-3] Equilibrium moisture content (EMC) is defined as that moisture content at which the wood is neither gaining nor losing moisture. EMC values at various levels of RH and temperature, suitable for most practical applications, are shown in Figure 4-1 and Table 4-2. These values have been calculated from Eq. 4-5, whose parameters W, K, K1 and K2 depend on temperature; Simpson (1973) showed that this equation provides a good fit to the EMC data tabulated in the 1955 edition of the Wood Handbook. An alternative equation for calculating EMC was presented by Glass and others (2014) (Eq. 4-6); equilibrium relative humidity can be calculated from EMC using its inverted form (Eq. 4-7). [p. 4-4] The level of precision (0.1% MC) in Table 4-2 is provided only for the purpose of illustrating trends; in reality, this level of precision is not meaningful. Actual EMC may vary considerably among wood species and among specimens of the same species; differences among species are generally minor at low and moderate relative humidity but become considerable at high RH. The Table 4-2 data set is suitable for practical applications but not reliable for scientific purposes such as thermodynamic analysis. [p. 4-5] At a given relative humidity level, the EMC for desorption is greater than the EMC for absorption (sorption hysteresis, Fig. 4-2). Strictly, desorption isotherms should be taken from full saturation; in practice, scanning desorption isotherms are commonly taken from samples initially equilibrated between 95% and 98% RH in absorption. EMC values in Table 4-2 were derived primarily for Sitka spruce under oscillating vapor pressure desorption, shown to represent a condition midway between absorption and desorption, and so provide a practical compromise when the direction of sorption is not known. Automated sorption balances (dynamic vapor sorption analyzers) are widely used; EMC measured with an often-reported stop criterion can be in error by as much as 1.25% MC at high RH. [p. 4-6] Multi-exponential decay analysis (MEDEA, Fig. 4-3) found two to five time constants in sorption kinetic data; measurements interrupted prior to equilibrium do not provide a reliable basis for understanding sorption kinetics.
key_points: EMC as a function of relative humidity (0 <= h <= 1) and temperature: Eq. 4-5, from which Table 4-2 and Figure 4-1 were calculated (p. 4-3)
Eq. 4-6 and 4-7 (Glass and others 2014) give an alternative EMC equation and its inverse for relative humidity (p. 4-3, 4-4)
Table 4-2's 0.1% precision only illustrates trends; species differences become considerable at high RH; the data are not reliable for scientific purposes (p. 4-4)
Desorption EMC is greater than absorption EMC at the same RH; Table 4-2 is midway, for Sitka spruce under oscillating vapor pressure desorption (p. 4-5)
sections.applicability: Estimating the moisture content wood will reach in service given ambient temperature and relative humidity, and vice versa (target-EMC design).

sections.title: Dimensional Stability / Shrinkage
sections.summary: Below the fiber saturation point wood shrinks and swells, tangentially about twice as much as radially and only slightly along the grain. Table 4-3 gives average radial, tangential and volumetric shrinkage of numerous domestic species (ASTM D143 methods) and Table 4-4 values collected from the world literature for selected imported species; shrinkage at moisture content x (Eq. 4-9) and conversions of specific gravity between moisture content bases (Eq. 4-10 to 4-13).
sections.body: [p. 4-7] Wood is dimensionally stable when the equilibrium moisture content is greater than the fiber saturation point. Below MCfs, wood changes dimension as it gains moisture (swells) or loses moisture (shrinks) because the volume of the cell wall depends on the amount of bound water; this can result in warping, checking, and splitting. Wood shrinks most in the direction of the annual growth rings (tangentially), about half as much across the rings (radially), and only slightly along the grain (longitudinally) (Fig. 4-4). Data have been collected to represent the average radial, tangential, and volumetric shrinkage of numerous domestic species by methods described in ASTM D143; shrinkage values, expressed as a percentage of the green dimension, are listed in Table 4-3. [p. 4-10] Shrinkage values collected from the world literature for selected imported species are listed in Table 4-4; [p. 4-9] its footnote states that they were obtained from world literature and may not represent a true species average. [p. 4-10] Transverse and volumetric shrinkage variability can be expressed by a coefficient of variation of approximately 15%. Longitudinal shrinkage from green to ovendry averages between 0.1% and 0.2% for most species; reaction wood and juvenile wood can shrink 2%, and such wood should be avoided in uses where longitudinal stability is important. Accurately predicting the shrinkage of an individual piece of wood is impossible (Fig. 4-6), but average shrinkage of a sufficient quantity of pieces can be predicted. Average shrinkage data in Tables 4-3 and 4-4 can be used to estimate shrinkage for a particular species if a great deal of accuracy is not required, assuming that shrinkage begins at the fiber saturation point MCfs and that dimensions decrease linearly with decreasing moisture content (Eq. 4-9). If MCfs is not known, 30% MC can be used as an approximation. Tangential values for S0 should be used for estimating width shrinkage of plainsawn material and radial values for quartersawn material; for mixed or unknown ring orientations, tangential values are suggested. [p. 4-11] Specific gravity Gx can be converted between moisture content bases with the volumetric shrinkage (Eq. 4-10) or found from basic specific gravity (Eq. 4-11); [p. 4-12] if S0 is not known it can be estimated from S0 = 26.5 Gb (Eq. 4-12), giving Eq. 4-13.
key_points: Tangential shrinkage is about twice radial; longitudinal shrinkage averages 0.1% to 0.2% green to ovendry, but reaction and juvenile wood can shrink 2% (p. 4-7, 4-10)

Table 4-3: average shrinkage of numerous domestic species by ASTM D143 methods; Table 4-4: values from the world literature for selected imported species, which may not represent a true species average (p. 4-7, 4-9, 4-10)
Shrinkage below MCfs assumed linear in moisture content (Eq. 4-9); 30% MC may be used if MCfs is not known; coefficient of variation about 15% (p. 4-10)
Specific gravity between moisture content bases: Eq. 4-10 to 4-13, with S0 = 26.5 Gb (Eq. 4-12) when S0 is not known (p. 4-11, 4-12)
sections.applicability: Estimating dimensional change of lumber/timber as moisture content changes -- critical for connection tolerances, gap detailing, and specific-gravity-dependent property adjustments.

sections.title: Density and Specific Gravity
sections.summary: Density of wood including water at a given moisture content, by three methods: from basic specific gravity (Eq. 4-14), from ovendry density and shrinkage (Eq. 4-15, with S0 from ovendry density by Eq. 4-16), or from Figure 4-7 and Table 4-6, whose values are based on Eq. 4-14.
sections.body: [p. 4-11] For wood, both mass and volume depend on moisture content. The density of ovendry wood ranges from about 160 kg m^-3 for balsa to more than 1,040 kg m^-3; a coefficient of variation of about 10% is considered suitable for describing the variability of ovendry density within common domestic species. Specific gravity of wood may be referenced to its volume at any moisture content, but in all cases G is based on ovendry mass (Table 4-5); ovendry mass and ovendry volume is the combination used in design specifications such as the NDS, and ovendry mass with green volume is basic specific gravity Gb. [p. 4-12] Methods for calculating density: Method 1, the specific gravity Gx from Eq. 4-11 or 4-13 with basic specific gravity from Table 5-3, 5-4, or 5-5, then density from Eq. 4-14; Method 2, density from ovendry density with Sx from Eq. 4-9 and S0 from Table 4-3 or 4-4 (Eq. 4-15), S0 being estimated from ovendry density by Eq. 4-16 if not known; Method 3, Figure 4-7 (which assumes fiber saturation at 30% MC and incorporates Eq. 4-9, 4-12 and 4-13) and Table 4-6, whose values are based on Eq. 4-14. The resulting value should be considered an approximation because of the inherent variability in the properties used.
key_points: Specific gravity is always based on ovendry mass; volume bases are ovendry (used in the NDS), green (basic, Gb) and 12% MC (p. 4-11)
Density at moisture content x: Eq. 4-14 (from Gx) or Eq. 4-15 (from ovendry density), or Figure 4-7 with Table 4-6, whose values are based on Eq. 4-14 (p. 4-12)
Coefficient of variation of ovendry density within common domestic species about 10% (p. 4-11)
sections.applicability: Computing wood self-weight and density-dependent properties at any in-service moisture content.

sections.title: Thermal Properties
sections.summary: Covers thermal conductivity (printed closed-form Eq 4-17 as a function of specific gravity and moisture content), heat capacity, thermal diffusivity, and coefficient of thermal expansion.
sections.body: [p. 4-12] Four important thermal properties of wood are thermal conductivity, heat capacity, thermal diffusivity, and coefficient of thermal expansion. [p. 4-13] The thermal conductivity of common structural woods is much less than the conductivity of metals with which wood often is mated in construction; it is about two to four times that of common insulating materials. The conductivity of structural softwood lumber at 12% moisture content is in the range of 0.10 to 0.14 W m^-1 K^-1, compared with 216 for aluminum, 45 for steel, 0.9 for concrete and 0.036 for mineral wool. Thermal conductivity increases as density, moisture content, temperature, or extractive content of the wood increases. Conductivity along the grain is greater than across the grain by a factor of 1.5 to 2.8, with an average of about 1.8. For Gx > 0.3, temperatures around 24 degrees C and moisture content below 25%, the conductivity across the grain is given by Eq. 4-17 with constants A, B and C. Heat capacity, thermal diffusivity, and coefficient of thermal expansion are covered in the following parts of the chapter with their own equations and Table 4-8.
key_points: Thermal conductivity k is estimated from specific gravity and MC via Eq 4-17
Along-grain conductivity is 1.5-2.8x cross-grain conductivity
Structural softwood k at 12% MC ~ 0.10-0.14 W/(m*K)
sections.applicability: Thermal/energy analysis of wood-framed assemblies (not a structural topic, included for completeness of the chapter's own equation set).

sections.title: Electrical Properties
sections.summary: DC and AC electrical properties of wood (resistivity, dielectric constant) are strongly moisture-dependent, forming the basis of resistance- and capacitance-type moisture meters.
sections.body: [p. 4-17] The electrical properties of wood depend strongly on moisture content, exhibiting changes that span almost 10 orders of magnitude over the range of possible moisture contents; electrical measurements have therefore been used to estimate moisture content. As the moisture content of wood increases from near zero to fiber saturation, conductivity can increase by a factor of over 10^10: about 10^-15 to 10^-16 S m^-1 for ovendry wood and 10^-3 to 10^-4 S m^-1 at fiber saturation; from fiber saturation to complete saturation the further increase is generally less than a hundredfold. Unlike conductivity of metals, the conductivity of wood increases with increasing temperature; it is greater along the grain than across the grain (approximate ratio 1.0:0.55:0.50 longitudinal, radial, tangential), and water-soluble salts such as preservative or fire-retardant treatment can substantially increase it. [p. 4-18] AC properties: at a given frequency, the real dielectric constant increases with temperature and moisture content (at 20 Hz from about 4 for dry wood to near 1 x 10^6 for wet wood). [p. 4-19] The power factor, used in alternating current (dielectric) moisture meters, varies from about 0.01 for dry, low-density woods to as large as 0.95 for dense woods at high moisture levels.
key_points: Electrical properties change by almost 10 orders of magnitude over the range of moisture content; conductivity rises by over 10^10 from near zero to fiber saturation (p. 4-17)
Wood conductivity increases with temperature and is greater along the grain (ratio about 1.0:0.55:0.50 L:R:T) (p. 4-17)
Dielectric constant and power factor depend on frequency, moisture content and temperature; the power factor is used in dielectric moisture meters (p. 4-18, 4-19)
sections.applicability: Moisture meters (resistance and dielectric types) and dielectric heating; not a structural design topic.

sections.title: Friction Properties
sections.summary: Coefficients of static and kinetic friction (Fig. 4-9) depend on wood moisture content, surface roughness and the opposing surface, and vary little with species except woods with abundant oily or waxy extractives; kinetic coefficients for smooth wood against hard, smooth surfaces range from 0.3 to 0.5 dry to 0.7 to 0.9 near fiber saturation.
sections.body: [p. 4-19] Figure 4-9 depicts the forces on an object: the coefficient of static friction is the maximum friction force divided by the normal force, and the coefficient of kinetic friction the friction force at constant sliding speed divided by the normal force. These coefficients depend on the moisture content of the wood, the roughness of the wood surface, and the characteristics of the opposing surface. They vary little with species except for woods that contain abundant oily or waxy extractives, such as lignumvitae. The coefficients of friction are an important safety consideration in applications such as wood decks and stairs. On most materials, the coefficients of friction for wood increase continuously as the moisture content increases from ovendry to fiber saturation, then remain about constant until considerable free water is present; when the surface is flooded with water, the coefficients of friction decrease. Coefficients of static friction are generally greater than those of kinetic friction. Coefficients of kinetic friction vary only slightly with speed when the wood moisture content is less than about 20%; at high moisture content, they decrease substantially as speed increases. Coefficients of kinetic friction for smooth, dry wood against hard, smooth surfaces commonly range from 0.3 to 0.5; [p. 4-20] at intermediate moisture content, 0.5 to 0.7; and near fiber saturation, 0.7 to 0.9.
key_points: Friction coefficients depend on wood moisture content, surface roughness and the opposing surface; they vary little with species except woods with abundant oily or waxy extractives (p. 4-19)
Friction rises from ovendry to fiber saturation and falls when the surface is flooded; an important safety consideration for decks and stairs (p. 4-19)
Kinetic friction, smooth wood on hard, smooth surfaces: 0.3 to 0.5 dry, 0.5 to 0.7 intermediate, 0.7 to 0.9 near fiber saturation (p. 4-19, 4-20)
sections.applicability: Sliding friction of wood surfaces, including slip safety of decks and stairs.

sections.title: Nuclear Radiation Properties
sections.summary: High-energy radiation techniques measure density and moisture content of wood: intensity falls as I = I0 exp(-mu z) (Eq. 4-30); gamma absorption varies directly with moisture content and density; neutrons measure hydrogen density and so moisture content; neutron activation analysis finds trace elements.
sections.body: [p. 4-20] Several techniques using high-energy radiation can be used to measure density and moisture content of wood. Radiation passing through matter is reduced in intensity according to I = I0 exp(-mu z) (Eq. 4-30), where I is the reduced intensity at depth z, I0 the incident intensity, and mu the linear absorption coefficient; divided by density it gives the mass absorption coefficient. The linear absorption coefficient of wood for gamma radiation varies directly with moisture content and density and inversely with the gamma ray energy (for ovendry yellow-poplar and 0.047-MeV gamma rays, about 0.065 to 0.11 cm^-1 over specific gravity 0.33 to 0.62). Beta absorption coefficients are larger, so even very thin wood products are virtually opaque to beta rays. Neutrons interact strongly with hydrogen, so lower energy neutrons measure the hydrogen density of a specimen and can be related to its moisture content; neutron activation analysis provides a sensitive nondestructive method for trace elements. Very large doses of gamma rays or neutrons can cause substantial degradation of wood (Chapter 5).
key_points: Radiation intensity: I = I0 exp(-mu z), Eq. 4-30; gamma absorption varies directly with moisture content and density (p. 4-20)
Lower energy neutrons measure hydrogen density and can be related to moisture content (p. 4-20)
sections.applicability: Nondestructive measurement of wood density and moisture content by radiation; not a structural design topic.
